questions.q: A nucleophile is a species that:
questions.solution:
A nucleophile **donates a lone pair** to an electron-deficient carbon — $\text{OH}^{-}$, $\text{CN}^{-}$, $\text{NH}_{3}$, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

It is attracted to the $\delta+$ carbon of a polar bond. An **electrophile** does the opposite.
options: donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre

questions.q: The order of rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes is:
questions.solution:
**Iodo fastest, fluoro slowest** — the order of **bond enthalpy**, not electronegativity.

C–I is the weakest bond ($238$ kJ/mol) and breaks most readily; C–F ($467$) is one of the strongest bonds in organic chemistry, which is why CFCs are so unreactive and so persistent.

questions.q: A halogenoalkane treated with hot ethanolic KOH gives:
questions.solution:
**Ethanolic** KOH and heat favour **elimination**, giving an alkene.

**Aqueous** KOH at lower temperature gives substitution and an alcohol. Same reagent, two different reactions — the **solvent** decides whether hydroxide acts as a nucleophile or as a base.

questions.q: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to:
questions.solution:
A **ketone**, and it stops there — there is no further hydrogen on the carbinol carbon to remove.

Primary alcohols give an aldehyde and then an acid; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation altogether.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by the time taken for turbidity?
questions.solution:
**Lucas reagent** — concentrated HCl with anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_{2}$.

Tertiary turns cloudy at once, secondary in about five minutes, primary only on heating — the order of carbocation stability, since the reaction goes by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.

questions.q: How many structural isomers of $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{7}\text{Br}$ are there?
How many alcohol isomers does $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH}$ have?
questions.solution:
Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol — $\mathbf{4}$.

Two primary, one secondary, one tertiary, which makes this the standard set for the Lucas test.

questions.q: How many chiral carbon atoms does 2-bromobutane have?
questions.solution:
Carbon 2 carries H, Br, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ — four different groups, so $\mathbf{1}$.

The compound therefore exists as a pair of enantiomers.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of ethanol, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$, in g/mol.
How many of these are oxidised by acidified dichromate: propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
questions.solution:
**Propan-1-ol** ✓ (primary $\to$ aldehyde $\to$ acid) and **propan-2-ol** ✓ (secondary $\to$ ketone).

**2-methylpropan-2-ol** ✗ — tertiary, with no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon.

So $\mathbf{2}$, and the orange-to-green colour change is the visible test.

questions.q: Compare the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ and $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ mechanisms in terms of steps, kinetics, stereochemistry and the substrate that favours each.
questions.solution:
**$\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ — one concerted step.**

The nucleophile attacks the $\delta+$ carbon from the **opposite side** to the leaving group, which departs as the new bond forms. The transition state has five groups around the carbon.

• **Kinetics:** rate $= k[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}]$ — **second order**, since both appear in the single step.

• **Stereochemistry:** **inversion** of configuration, like an umbrella blown inside out.

• **Favoured by:** **primary** halides, where the back of the carbon is accessible.

**$\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ — two steps.**

**Step 1 (slow):** the C–X bond breaks heterolytically, giving a **carbocation**.

**Step 2 (fast):** the nucleophile attacks the cation.

• **Kinetics:** rate $= k[\text{RX}]$ — **first order**. The nucleophile's concentration has no effect, because it is not in the slow step.

• **Stereochemistry:** the carbocation is **planar**, so attack from either face gives a **racemic mixture**.

• **Favoured by:** **tertiary** halides, whose carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups — and whose back is completely blocked to $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ attack.

**Secondary halides do both**, in proportions depending on the conditions.

**The experimental test.** Double the nucleophile concentration: an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ rate doubles, an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ rate does not move. Kinetics and stereochemistry agree, which is what makes the two mechanisms believable rather than merely plausible.

**Solvent matters too:** polar protic solvents stabilise the carbocation and favour $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile bare and reactive, favouring $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$.

questions.q: Give four reactions of halogenoalkanes with the reagents and products, and explain the synthetic value of each.
questions.solution:
**1. With aqueous KOH (warm) — hydrolysis.**

$\text{RBr} + \text{OH}^{-} \to \text{ROH} + \text{Br}^{-}$

Gives an **alcohol**, and so opens the whole of alcohol chemistry.

**2. With ethanolic KOH (hot) — elimination.**

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br} + \text{KOH} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}_{2} + \text{KBr} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Gives an **alkene**. The same reagent in a different solvent — hydroxide acts as a **base** here rather than a nucleophile.

**3. With ethanolic KCN, heated under reflux.**

$\text{RBr} + \text{CN}^{-} \to \text{RCN} + \text{Br}^{-}$

**This adds a carbon to the chain** — one of the few reactions that lengthens a carbon skeleton, which makes it valuable in synthesis.

The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

**4. With excess ammonia in a sealed tube.**

$\text{RBr} + 2\text{NH}_{3} \to \text{RNH}_{2} + \text{NH}_{4}\text{Br}$

Gives an **amine** — but the product is itself nucleophilic and reacts further, so excess ammonia is used to favour the primary amine.

**5. With silver nitrate in ethanol** — the standard test, giving a precipitate whose colour identifies the halogen and whose rate of appearance shows the C–X bond strength.

**The pattern:** the halogen makes the carbon $\delta+$, and everything follows from that. Halogenoalkanes are rarely useful in themselves; they are the crossroads of organic synthesis.

questions.q: Describe the oxidation of alcohols, explaining how the product depends on the class of alcohol and on the conditions, and describe how the products are identified.
questions.solution:
**The reagent** is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), which turns from **orange to green** as $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ forms.

**Primary alcohol — two stages, and the conditions decide which you get.**

$\text{RCH}_{2}\text{OH} \to \text{RCHO} \to \text{RCOOH}$

• **Distil off** the product as it forms, and the **aldehyde** is collected — it boils lower than the alcohol, having no hydrogen bonding, and escapes before it can be oxidised further.

• **Heat under reflux** with excess oxidant, and the **carboxylic acid** is obtained — reflux returns the aldehyde to the flask to be oxidised again.

That distinction between distillation and reflux is worth a mark in itself.

**Secondary alcohol.** Gives a **ketone**, and stops there. There is no hydrogen left on the carbinol carbon, and further oxidation would mean breaking a C–C bond.

**Tertiary alcohol.** **No reaction** — no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon at all. The solution stays orange, which is itself a useful test.

**Identifying the products.**

• **Aldehyde against ketone:** Tollens' reagent gives a **silver mirror** with an aldehyde only; Fehling's gives a **red-brown** precipitate with an aliphatic aldehyde only.

• **Carboxylic acid:** effervescence with sodium carbonate, giving $\text{CO}_{2}$ which turns limewater milky.

• **Both aldehydes and ketones** give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, whose melting point identifies the specific compound.

**A summary worth memorising:** primary gives aldehyde then acid, secondary gives ketone, tertiary gives nothing.

questions.q: Explain optical isomerism, state the conditions for it, and explain why an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ reaction gives a racemic product while $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ does not.
questions.solution:
**Optical isomers (enantiomers)** are non-superimposable mirror images, like a pair of hands.

They are identical in melting point, boiling point and every ordinary chemical property — differing only in **rotating plane-polarised light** equally in opposite directions, and in how they react with **other chiral molecules**.

**The condition:** a **chiral centre** — a carbon atom bonded to **four different groups**.

**A racemic mixture** is equal amounts of both, and is **optically inactive** because the rotations cancel.

**Why $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ racemises.** The first step forms a **carbocation**, which is $sp^{2}$ hybridised and **planar**.

Whatever chirality the starting material had is destroyed at that instant. The nucleophile can then attack either face with equal ease, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers.

**Why $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ does not.** There is no intermediate. The nucleophile attacks from the side **opposite** the leaving group, and the other three groups flip through like an umbrella in the wind.

The product is a **single enantiomer**, with the configuration **inverted**.

**Why this matters far beyond the examination.** Biological molecules — enzymes, receptors, DNA — are all chiral, so they interact differently with the two enantiomers of a drug.

One may be therapeutic and the other inactive or harmful, as the thalidomide tragedy showed. Modern drugs are therefore developed and tested as **single enantiomers**, which is why asymmetric synthesis is such a large field.

questions.q: Describe how you would prepare and purify a sample of 1-bromobutane from butan-1-ol in the laboratory.
questions.solution:
**The reaction.** HBr is generated in situ from sodium bromide and concentrated sulphuric acid — it is a gas, and inconvenient to handle directly:

$\text{NaBr} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \to \text{NaHSO}_{4} + \text{HBr}$

$\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH} + \text{HBr} \to \text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Procedure.**

1. Mix butan-1-ol with sodium bromide and add concentrated sulphuric acid **slowly, with cooling** — the mixing is strongly exothermic.

2. **Heat under reflux** for about $45$ minutes. The reflux condenser returns the volatile reagents and product to the flask instead of letting them escape.

3. **Distil** off the crude product, which comes over as a cloudy liquid below $105$°C.

**Purification.**

4. **Separating funnel.** Wash with water to remove acid and soluble impurities, then with sodium carbonate solution to neutralise the remaining acid — **release the pressure frequently**, as $\text{CO}_{2}$ is given off. The product is the **lower** layer, being denser than water.

5. **Dry** over anhydrous sodium sulphate or calcium chloride until the liquid is clear, then decant.

6. **Redistil**, collecting the fraction at the boiling point of 1-bromobutane, $101$–$104$°C.

**Identifying and checking the product:** measure the boiling point, and test with silver nitrate in ethanol for a cream precipitate of AgBr.

**Why the yield is always well below theoretical:** losses at every transfer, some elimination to butene as a side reaction, and the reaction being an equilibrium that never goes fully to completion.
